messages.author: 6d3f7222550fe21b
messages.subject: quoted class in ddply, not in melt
parts:
ddply knows about the "quoted" class, which has the consequence (I think) that one can use the following syntax to tell it which variables to use for splitting:

# Try printing
.( myonefactor, myotherfactor)

# Turn this into something more familiar:
unlist(lapply(.( myonefactor, myotherfactor), paste))

# Example of how this strange thing works:

junk<-data.frame( pig=c("ee", "ee", "onk", "onk", "onk"), dog=c("uff", "arg", "uff", "arg", "snarl"))
#
junk<-rbind(junk, junk[2:4,])
junk$Y<-rnorm(nrow(junk))
require(ggplot2)
# An older way to think about it:
ddply(junk, c("pig", "dog"), function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF), mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )
# The "quoted class" way:
ddply(junk, .(pig, dog) , function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF), mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )

# This seems to be related to the fact that the arguments of ddply (their names) all start with a dot....?
# This syntax does not work however in melt. The old way works:
melt(junk, id.vars=c("pig", "dog"))
# but the new way generates an error:
melt(junk, id.vars=.(pig, dog))

# What's the thinking here?

parts:
On Mon, Apr 18, 2011 at 4:33 PM, Jacob Wegelin <jacobw...@fastmail.fm> wrote:
>
> ddply knows about the "quoted" class, which has the consequence (I think)
> that one can use the following syntax to tell it which variables to use for
> splitting:
>
> # Try printing
> .( myonefactor, myotherfactor)
>
> # Turn this into something more familiar:
> unlist(lapply(.( myonefactor, myotherfactor), paste))
>
> # Example of how this strange thing works:
>
> junk<-data.frame( pig=c("ee", "ee", "onk", "onk", "onk"), dog=c("uff",
> "arg", "uff", "arg", "snarl"))
> # junk<-rbind(junk, junk[2:4,])
> junk$Y<-rnorm(nrow(junk))
> require(ggplot2)
> # An older way to think about it:
> ddply(junk, c("pig", "dog"), function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF),
> mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )
> # The "quoted class" way:
> ddply(junk, .(pig, dog) , function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF),
> mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )

But . does much more than that:

f <- function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF), mean=mean(STUFF$Y))

ddply(junk, .(dog = pig, pig = dog), f)
ddply(junk, .(substr(pig, 1, 2)), f)
ddply(junk, .(pi = substr(pig, 1, 2)), f)

> # This seems to be related to the fact that the arguments of ddply (their
> names) all start with a dot....?
That's just a coincidence.

> # This syntax does not work however in melt. The old way works:
> melt(junk, id.vars=c("pig", "dog"))
> # but the new way generates an error:
> melt(junk, id.vars=.(pig, dog))
>
> # What's the thinking here?

Basically, it makes sense to aggregate by computed values, but I don't
think that it makes sense to melt by computed values.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: quoted class in ddply, not in melt
parts:
Dear Hadley,

Thank you for your email on this subject.

As you develop and redesign the libraries, do you plan to document the "." function?

It seems that "." needs a help file that will plainly state *what it is intended for* and (on a more detail-oriented or nerdy plane) exactly what it does in terms of arguments and value returned. Like the traditional R help files.

By trial and error, I think I figured out that "." saves us from having to type quotation marks. But is that its point?

If I understand your post, you say that "." is also a way to rename the columns of a data frame.

If I want to rename the "pig" column to "pi", I do the following, which makes things explicit.

names(junk)[names(junk)=="pig"] <-"pi"

As an end-user, I am puzzled by why these operations (placing double quotes around strings and renaming columns of a dataframe) would be combined into a single function and why the function would be called dot (".") rather than an evocative mnemonic name.

One of my goals in writing R code is that I want to understand a year later what my code is supposed to do. I am scared to call a mysterious or obscure function because later on I might never figure out how my function works.

And a dot is very easy to miss if I'm reading through code. And one false keystroke would delete it.

But you must have something in mind with the "dot" function. It must be part of a more general plan for these libraries? And you must have a darn good reason you call it dot?

Just my feedback

messages.author: 68b661fcb57b94a9
messages.subject: lines indicating bin widths in geom_histogram
parts:
ggplot2 users:

Is there an option or work around for including in a histogram vertical lines that show explicitly the delineation between bins?

For example:

tst<-data.frame(age=rnorm(2000,50,30))

ggplot(tst,aes(age))+geom_histogram(alpha=.3)

The above produces a histogram, but without vertical lines within the histogram that indicate the boundaries of the bins. Is there a means for doing this? Thanks very much for your help.  




Adam Loveland

parts:
Hi Ista,

Thank you. That worked!


Group,

Unfortunately, having solved that issue, I've now run into a new one that escapes my intuition. Looking at the example below, it should be fairly clear what I'm trying to do. But two distinct problems get in my way:

1. How can I label a negative value in the appropriate position with its absolute value?
2. How can I apply a label format (e.g. comma) in conjunction with the absolute value function (i.e. geom_text(aes(label=comma(abs(x)))) doesn't seem to work)?

Below is where the solution stands now, with neither issue 1 or 2 solved:

 tst<-data.frame(age=rnorm(2000,50,30),gender=c(rep("f",1000),rep("m",1000)))

ggplot(data=subset(tst), aes(age)) +
geom_bar(data=subset(tst,gender=="f"),stat="bin",colour="pink",alpha=.3)+
geom_bar(data=subset(tst,gender=="m"),stat="bin",aes(y=-..count..),colour="blue",alpha=.3)+
coord_flip()+
theme_bw()+
geom_text(data=subset(tst,gender=="f"),stat="bin",aes(label=abs(..count..)),hjust=1)+
geom_text(data=subset(tst,gender=="m"),stat="bin",aes(label=abs(-..count..)),hjust=1)

Obviously, I'm in no way tied to using geom_bar - maybe geom_ribbon is the way to go here? But I think in any case, there is the requirement to label negative values with absolute values, positioned appropriately, as well as the need to apply a format (comma) function in addition to the abs function. And neither of these I've been able to figure out how to do.

Thanks for your help !  



Adam Loveland
